extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and writing weather stories and related news (storms, seasonal changes, eclipses) for newspapers, with advice on subject selection, tone, data, human-interest detail, and contextualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence of official forecasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Official forecasts of the weather are given a place of prominence on the front page of most papers, and are read with interest by most readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place official forecasts prominently (front page). Recognize that most readers consult forecasts and that forecasts are a staple of daily news; ensure forecasts are timely and clearly presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather story subject selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of the seasons, extremes of heat and cold, storms, and unusual weather of any sort serve as subjects for weather stories. Two stories of an eclipse of the sun have been included in this division, although such phenomena should be classed as astronomical rather than meteorological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose stories from seasonal changes, extreme events, storms, unusual/local phenomena and, where relevant, astronomical events (e.g., eclipses) — noting classification differences. Match the subject to reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of treatment: informative or lighter/humorous
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the purely informative type of story is the usual one for weather, the subject may be treated in a lighter vein. There is often a chance for life and color whether the treatment be informative or more or less humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide tone based on audience and outlet: standard informative reporting for forecasts and impacts; lighter, colorful or humorous treatments for features. Either approach should aim to inject 'life and color' into the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specific measurements and forecasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Report concrete temperature readings and forecasts (e.g., 'temperature reading is only 41° in the middle of the day', 'lowest temperature reading... 39').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include precise numerical data (temperatures, times, durations) and forecaster predictions to substantiate claims. Provide minimum/maximum readings and comparisons when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain meteorological causes and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain causes such as areas of high barometric pressure moving eastward, which account for unusual temperatures or patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote forecasters and meteorological experts and give concise explanations of why the weather is behaving as it is (e.g., pressure systems, fronts). This helps readers understand causes and likely short-term developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate weather to readers' health, business and pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The universal interest in the weather... is due to its effect upon health, business, and pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories around practical impacts: health risks (frosts), business interruptions (stores, transport), and leisure/pleasure (park visits, festivals). Make explicit how readers' daily lives are affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include vivid human-interest detail and scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: There is often a chance for life and color... whether the treatment be informative or more or less humorous (e.g., descriptions of couples in the park, squirrels surprised by crowds, vendors of balloons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anecdotes, sensory description, and specific human moments to enliven weather pieces. Include crowd behavior, local color, and small scenes that make the report relatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe operational and logistical effects in storms
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on damage to property, interruptions to transport and services, and emergency/official responses (e.g., derelict walls falling, trolley lines, plows, telephone exchange loads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail which services and infrastructure are affected, how agencies responded (plows, police, firemen), specific damage examples, and any disruptions to schedules or commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document casualties, rescues and human cost accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: Include casualties, injuries, deaths, rescue operations and the conditions leading to loss of life (e.g., people dying in pits from smoke; bargemen drowned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide numbers, circumstances, rescue attempts, and humane descriptions of aftermath while maintaining factual precision and sensitivity. Use official sources when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name and quote officials and experts; include titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify forecasters, astronomers, military officers and leaders by name and title (e.g., 'Prof. W. S. Eichelberger', 'Forecaster Smith', 'Maj. P. J. Hamrock') and report their statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute information to named experts/officials with titles. Include direct quotes or summarized statements and, where relevant, translations (e.g., translated speeches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include precise timing and instrumentation for astronomical events
rubrics_metrics.description: Report exact times of contact and observation for eclipses and note instruments and photographic efforts (e.g., 'first contact... thirty-five minutes and twenty-eight seconds after 9 o'clock', 'photographs were taken by a forty-foot photo-heliograph').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For astronomical/technical phenomena provide exact timings, locations, observational details, instrumentation used, and the percentage or character of the event (partial vs total) to satisfy scientifically minded readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tone and presentation to the outlet/audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The same facts about the same eclipse are given in different ways in the Washington Herald (straight/informative) and the Washington Post (lighter/humorous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor voice, level of technicality, and rhetorical approach to the publication and its readers. A single event can be covered with varying degrees of formality or wit depending on audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide historical comparisons and precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Use past records and historical data to contextualize current events (e.g., listing notable April snowfalls from 1821, 1852, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring in historical measurements and notable past events to show whether current weather is exceptional and to add depth to the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give practical advice and warnings when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Warn of potential damage (e.g., frost danger to fruit trees and gardens) and suggest protective actions ('housewives may as well keep their blankets on the beds').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When weather creates actionable risk, include clear, practical guidance for readers on how to protect property, crops, or health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize timeliness and chronological sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use immediate time markers and sequence events (e.g., 'this morning', 'early yesterday', 'as the day progressed') to structure breaking or developing stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize reporting chronologically for clarity on unfolding events; lead with the most recent/important facts and use timestamps for precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document logistics and numbers in conflict/incident reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting clashes or incidents include troop/militia positions, numbers, ammunition shipments, train movements and specific locations (e.g., 'Five thousand rounds were taken to the troops...', '400 strikers await...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete logistical details (quantities, movements, locations) and sources for them; these specifics lend credibility and allow readers to grasp scale.
